purpose: Azathioprine is used to calm down an overactive immune system. It is commonly used to prevent your body from rejecting a transplanted organ, and it also helps treat autoimmune conditions like rheumatoid arthritis, lupus, and inflammatory bowel disease. Basically, it helps keep your immune system from attacking your own body or a new organ.
how_it_works: Your immune system uses special cells called white blood cells to fight threats. Azathioprine works by slowing down the production of these cells, which keeps your immune system from being too aggressive. Think of it like turning down the volume on an overreacting alarm system so it stops causing damage.
common_side_effects: Nausea, vomiting, and upset stomach are the most common, especially when you first start taking it. You may also notice loss of appetite, diarrhea, or feeling unusually tired. Some people develop mouth sores or mild skin rashes.
warnings: Because this medication lowers your immune system, you are more likely to get infections, so let your doctor know right away if you develop a fever or feel sick. Long-term use slightly increases the risk of certain cancers, including skin cancer, so use sunscreen and protect your skin outdoors. Avoid live vaccines while taking this medication, and never stop taking it without talking to your doctor first.
typical_dosing: The dose is very individual and based on your weight, your condition, and how your body responds. It is usually taken once or twice daily by mouth, with food to help reduce stomach upset. Your doctor will start you on a low dose and adjust it over time based on blood test results.
